Whereas the ideal experiment to examine separate effects of mood and distraction would be to manipulate mood while controlling for distraction in one condition, and to manipulate distraction while controlling for mood in another condition, the design of Jefferies et al. does allow for exploring the hypothesis that distraction in itself (regardless of mood) diminishes the AB effect. decisions.reason: Olivers and Nieuwenhuis (2005) reported the empirical finding that concurrent task-irrelevant mental activity—specifically listening to an irrelevant beat/music or ruminating about events (a holiday or dinner groceries)—diminishes the attentional blink (AB) effect relative to no distraction. In Aim 4 and Results Section 1.5.2 (Table 5), Tibboel explicitly tests this distraction effect by comparing all experimental MIP conditions (in which participants ruminated on emotional events and listened to music throughout the AB task, N=124) against the control condition (no MIP and no music during the AB task, N=33). Although conducted within the dataset collected to replicate Jefferies et al. (2008) (shipped row 1144) and labeled exploratory, a changed manipulation or shared dataset does not exclude an explicit conceptual retest of a published empirical finding. Moreover, Jefferies et al. (2008) reassigned control participants by mood ratings and never compared the distracted music/MIP groups against the non-distracted control group, so row 1144 does not represent or supersede this target in a replication chain.

Olivers and Nieuwenhuis (2005, 2006) suggested that this limitation is not structural, but is instead due to poor allocation of attentional resources. According to their overinvestment hypothesis, the AB effect is due to an overinvestment of attentional resources into processing of T1. This leaves insufficient resources to also process T2 when it is presented quickly after T1. In order to examine this, they altered participants’ mental state by providing them with distraction and examined effects of this manipulation on AB performance. Olivers and Nieuwenhuis (2005) found that participants who listened to an irrelevant beat and participants who thought about their holiday or the groceries needed for a dinner with friends showed a smaller AB effect (i.e. improved T2 accuracy on shorter lags). Similarly, the same authors (2006) found that the AB effect was diminished for participants who were presented with affectively positive pictures during the AB task. decisions.reason: Unlike Olivers and Nieuwenhuis (2005), which reported the diminished AB effect under concurrent music/beat listening and rumination, Tibboel explicitly identifies Olivers and Nieuwenhuis (2006) as reporting a diminished AB effect when participants were presented with affectively positive pictures during the AB task (chunk 6) and as hypothesising a theoretical link between mood/positive affect and attentional overinvestment (chunk 12). Tibboel does not present affectively positive pictures during the AB task. In Aim 4 (chunk 13) and Section 1.5.2 (chunks 32-34), Tibboel explicitly notes that her design cannot isolate mood while controlling for distraction and therefore tests distraction in itself regardless of mood by comparing the music/MIP conditions against the no-music/no-MIP control condition (which retests the 2005 concurrent music/rumination finding, target_index 1). To the extent Tibboel tests mood or positive affect (happy MIP) on the AB task, the closest study in the replication chain actually retested is Jefferies et al. (2008) (shipped row 1144), while joint citations of 2006 for the general overinvestment theory are theoretical framing.

Moreover, the poor phonological decoders with DD not only demonstrated less sensitivity to the FD illusion compared to the typical reading age- and IQ-matched group (supporting Pammer and Wheatley, 2001 ), but also to a reading-level and IQ-matched control group. decisions.reason: As verified in primary context 0041, Olulade et al. (2013) reported two key empirical components supporting their conclusion that magnocellular-dorsal (M-D) visual dysfunction is a consequence of reading deprivation rather than a cause of developmental dyslexia (DD): (1) in Experiment 2, the M-D deficit found against chronological-age controls disappeared when 12 dyslexic children were compared with 12 younger reading-level and IQ-matched controls (F(1,22)=0.01, p=.938), and (2) in Experiment 3, reading intervention increased V5/MT activity. In Experiment 2 of the current paper, Gori et al. (2014) specifically introduce a younger reading-level and IQ-matched control group (N=10) compared against dyslexic poor phonological decoders (N=8; plus merged ANOVA) on M-D sensitivity (frequency-doubling threshold, t(16)=2.962, p<.05) to test whether the M-D deficit persists relative to reading-level controls, and explicitly contrast this finding with Olulade et al. (2013). Using subcortical FD perimetry rather than cortical V5/MT fMRI and not retesting Experiment 3's intervention do not exclude this conceptual retest of Olulade et al.'s reading-level-matched comparison. Shipped row 697 (Pammer & Wheatley, 2001) tested only chronological-age controls.

decisions.reason: Waldeyer and Roelle (2020/2021) explicitly design and test their first hypothesis ('replication hypothesis') as a conceptual replication of the delayed-keyword effect on relative metacomprehension accuracy: comparing delayed generation of five keywords per text against a no-keyword control group using within-person Goodman-Kruskal gamma correlations between JOLs and posttest scores (t(93)=2.06, p=.021), and explicitly name De Bruin et al. (2011) in their replication verdict (chunk 45) and measure definition (chunk 29). As verified in primary context 0041, De Bruin et al. (2011) directly tested a delayed-keyword versus no-keyword control design on within-person gamma relative metacomprehension accuracy across two experiments with 6th/7th and 4th graders, reporting significantly higher relative accuracy for 6th and 7th graders as a distinct empirical finding prior to and separate from study regulation. Omitting the downstream regulation measure in the current study or testing university students does not exclude a conceptual retest of the relative-accuracy component. Shipped row 139 (Thiede et al., 2005) is a separate U.S. college paper that primarily contrasted delayed against immediate keyword/thinking/yoked conditions.

decisions.reason: As verified in the complete primary PDF in 0041, Thiede, Anderson, and Therriault (2003) conducted a single experiment (N=66 UIC college students) comparing delayed keyword generation (five keywords per text after reading all texts), immediate keyword generation, and a no-keyword control group, reporting significantly higher relative monitoring accuracy (within-person Goodman-Kruskal gamma between JOLs and initial test performance, F(2,63)=4.07) before restudy choices and second-test learning. Waldeyer and Roelle (2020/2021) directly adopt Thiede et al.'s (2003) pre-reading keyword instruction and Titanic example (chunks 33-34), retest the delayed-keyword versus no-keyword control contrast on within-person gamma relative accuracy (chunks 29, 37-38), and explicitly cite Thiede et al. (2003) in their successful replication conclusion (chunk 45). Not testing the downstream restudy/regulation stage (noted in Limitations, chunk 56) does not exclude the directly retested relative-accuracy component. Moreover, 0041 confirms that shipped row 139 (Thiede et al., 2005) reports four separate experiments (N=132, 100, 54, 60) testing lag/spacing/thinking/yoked mechanisms rather than the same cohort or report as 2003.

decisions.reason: Waldeyer and Roelle (2020/2021) cite Thiede, Redford, Wiley, and Griffin (2017) (10.1111/bjep.12166) alongside De Bruin et al. (2011) and Thiede et al. (2003, 2005) when describing prior studies of the delayed-keyword effect and stating their replication conclusion for relative metacomprehension accuracy (chunks 2, 5, 8, 45), but omitted it when listing prior studies for the intra-individual gamma relative-accuracy measure in the Method section (chunk 29). As documented in primary context 0041, only the structured abstract of Thiede et al. (2017) is accessible; that abstract describes 480 seventh-grade students assigned to restudy selection conditions (participant-chosen, test-based, and judgment-based selection) and their post-restudy comprehension gains, without mentioning a delayed-keyword versus no-keyword manipulation or a relative-accuracy condition contrast. Because the full text of Thiede et al. (2017) is unavailable, the evidence neither establishes nor excludes whether the 2017 article contains an empirically tested delayed-keyword relative-accuracy finding (or whether it shares a cohort/report chain with earlier studies or is cited merely as broad background).
